clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's death, 1991–1994
clusters.reason: Around your grandfather's stroke in June 1991, within three years: you left home for the conservatory that September, leaned hard on your roommate Rafe, hurt your wrist in the first term and lost your footing, the two of you clashed and he moved out, you withdrew into your room getting high and absorbed in radios, and by early 1992 you were lost and low, unable to get going. Your mother filled in your college forms and you let it happen. You dropped out and spent a bleak year at the community college shooting pool at night and sleeping by day. An exchange to Portugal in early 1994 snapped you out of it; you tore through the rest of your degree and found your drive again. Your shifts pile up from his death through your recovery, each one near another's.

clusters.name: Your father Russell's marriage to Bettina, 1974–1987
clusters.reason: From when your parents first separated in early 1974 through your early teens: your father became a couple with Bettina around 1976 and married her in 1984, and you moved into the rebuilt house with them and Desmond's children in 1989. You had clashed with your stepfather from around 1987, and your bond with your father was warm though you were forever angling for his notice. Your anxiety spiked when you made the city chess squad in 1987, out of your depth. You liked late nights through secondary school and by 1989 were unsure whether that was out of the ordinary. Late nights would dog you; these days you need pills to sleep. Your shifts in relationship to both your father and stepfather, and your own growing anxiety and symptom, cluster around the years when your father's partnership with Bettina was settling and reshaping your household.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Lorna's death, 2008–2010
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother's death in January 2008, within two years: you were four weeks building at Alder Creek with Silas before nursing school, too drained for conversation with your mother; she pressed you to visit and you kept the door shut on her. You left for nursing school in Marlow Sound that August and stopped speaking to your mother—the silence held roughly a year. Your aunt Imogen had a stroke in early 2009 with months of rehabilitation. Your partner's brother Leo returned nearby in August 2019 with his family. Within this span, you left for and began the nursing programme. Your shift from distance to cutoff with your mother, her anxiety pressing toward you, the stroke in the extended family, and your own move away cluster around your grandmother's death and your entry into nursing school.

clusters.name: Your marriage to Wren, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: From your marriage in March 2017 through October 2019: you saw your mother a bit less once Wren came along. Your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in October 2017. Your sister Tara married James and they settled in Rennick for her airline work; their first grandchild was due later that autumn. Your job steadied and paid well by June 2019, but you constantly felt you ought to be driving your projects forward; you started a sleeping pill. Your aunt Imogen's memory was slipping and worsening; she lashed out when muddled with her son Hal. In late October 2019, Wren was swamped one thing after another—a street party, a fundraising dinner, then the drive to the lake for her mother's retirement. You were too strict laying out a plan to settle her; she talked with her father and brother all day, nothing happening to one that the others didn't hear. Once the weekend had a plan she settled and the dinner went well. But awake from the small hours at the lake weekend, you had no more sleep and could only pull back as the others rose; your sleep is at its worst around her family. Your shifts in anxiety and your moves toward and away from your mother, the overfunctioning in your partnership, and the extended-family illnesses cluster around the years when your marriage and Wren's family closeness were reshaping your household.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Winifred's cancer diagnosis, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother's bowel cancer found in 2001 or 2002, within three years: you were running out of steam for performing, less content by the month. Your grandmother's operations were followed by chemotherapy. You had a disastrous audition for the national orchestra in your home town and were done with performing, casting about for what came next; you draw a near-total blank on family life across those years. You were on poor terms with family and friends and left Thornbury for Gull Harbour, then met Marisol at a winter party and left for Fenwick to live with her, then split up within the year. You sank into a deep depression once they split, and at the bottom you hardly moved from the sofa. You returned to Thornbury after the split and the depression and could not face your family; they seemed a world away from what you were going through. You relied, gingerly, on friends—Corbin, Dale, and Hamish. Your father and Corbin talked several times during your stay. You began swimming laps to help you sleep and requested help from your parents with therapy costs; you returned to your therapist Victor Halloran. Your last visit with your grandmother was brief and hung over on the way to the airport; you cut it short and regret it. She died in February 2004. Your shifts from high functioning to deep depression, your moves away from and toward different people, the failed relationship, and your return to therapy cluster over the years your grandmother was ill and died.

periods.name: the year I left home
periods.words: The first is the year I left home: I went off to the conservatory, hurt my wrist in the first term and couldn't play, dropped out and drifted at my mother's place, then spent a bleak spell at the community college shooting pool every night until an exchange in Portugal snapped me out of it and I tore through the rest of my coursework.

periods.name: the long slump
periods.words: The second is the long slump, roughly ages 27 to 29, when nothing at home felt right, I moved to Gull Harbour away from nearly everyone I knew, then followed Marisol to Fenwick, and when that fell apart I went under, a depression I only really climbed out of after nursing school.
